newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean stocks soar, helped by crumbling strikes.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean stocks soar, helped by crumbling strikes.

text.p: South Korean stocks soared on Tuesday, partly in jubilation over crumbling strikes and expectations the government would step in with measures to boost the market, brokers and analysts said.
The composite index closed at 686.59 points, up 4.1 percent or 27.05 points on the day. Advancing stocks overwhelmed losers 769 to 81, with 60 stocks remaining unchanged.

"Investors now have a sort of immunity to the strikes as they have lasted for a long time. Today the crisis was expected to deepen, but the reality was different," Park Byung-moon, head of sales at LG Securities, told Reuters.

"Investors think the impact from the strikes has already been reflected on the stock prices. Strikes are more than offset by improving market fundamentals," said a Ssangyong Investment and Securities broker.

South Korea's export-driven industries have been idle since a series of wildcat strikes began in protest against the passing of a new labour law that is designed to make the local labour market more flexible.
Key blue chips, most of them heavily dependent on exports, closed sharply higher. Chipmaker Samsung Electronics Co was up 3,500 won to 47,500 and Hyundai Motor Co added 1,800 won to close at 24,500.
Speculation swept the bourse that the government would soon announce market-boosting steps, including an early expansion of the ceiling on foreign share ownership.
The government has pledged to raise the ceiling by three percentage points this year from the current 20 percent, but no time frame has been set. Officials denied an announcement would be made soon.

Stocks tumbled about 10 percent at the start of the strikes but regained lost ground early last week, led by financial shares that rose on talk that mergers and acquisitions could become active in banks and brokerages.
That speculation was sparked by President Kim Young-sam who said last week a panel would be set up to oversee restructuring of the financial industry. Details have yet to be drawn up.
A slowdown in the economy and an overhang of loans used for margin trading dampened sentiment on South Korean stocks in 1996. The market fell 26.9 percent to end the year at 651.22.

The Federation of Korean Trade Unions had called out its 1.2 million members on Tuesday for a two-day strike to try to force the government to dump the new labour law which allows firms to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
They were to be joined on Wednesday by members of the 500,000-strong Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has vowed an indefinite walkout against the law.
But buses and subway trains were running almost normally on Tuesday while the number of taxis on the street fell slightly.

Brokers said signs of improving market fundamentals, such as an increase in customer deposits with brokerages, had boosted sentiment. Many investors had sold shares in the last six months to pay loans to brokerages falling due.

Outstanding margin loans have fallen to 2.56 trillion won ($3 billion) from around 2.8 trillion late last year, while customer deposits have steadily grown to 2.58 trillion won from around 2.4 trillion.
